exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Unit Rate as the Quotient of an Integer and a Fraction

question.text: Suzie takes $\dfrac{2}{3}$ hours to read $22$ pages of a certain book. How many pages can she read in $1$ hour?
question.explanation:
To find the number of pages Suzie can read in $1$ hour, we compute the unit rate of pages per hour. We do this by dividing the number of pages Suzie reads, $22,$ by the number of hours, $\dfrac{2}{3},$ as follows:

\[ 22\div \dfrac{2}{3} \]

Dividing a fraction by a whole number is equivalent to multiplying the fraction by the reciprocal of that whole number:

\begin{align} 22\div \dfrac{2}{3}&= 22 \times \dfrac{3}{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{22}{1} \times \dfrac{3}{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{22 \times 3}{1 \times 2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{66}{2}\\[5pt] &=33 \end{align}

Therefore, Suzie can read $33$ pages in $1$ hour.

question.text: A skydiver falls $40$ feet in $\dfrac 56$ seconds. What is the unit rate of feet fallen per second?
question.explanation:
To compute the unit rate of feet per second, we divide the number of feet, $40,$ by the number of seconds, $\dfrac 56$, as follows:

\[ 40 \div \dfrac 56 \]

To divide by a fraction, we multiply by the fraction's reciprocal:

\begin{align} 40\div \dfrac 56&= 40\times \dfrac{6}{5} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{40}{1} \times \dfrac{6}{5} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{40 \times 6}{1 \times 5} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{240}{5} \\[5pt] &= 48 \end{align}

Therefore, the unit rate in this situation is $48$ feet per second.

example.title: Calculating a Unit Rate as the Quotient of an Integer and a Fraction

question.text: A leaking paddling pool loses $6$ liters of water in $\dfrac23$ hours. How much water will it lose in $1$ hour?
question.explanation:
To find out how much water the pool will lose in $1$ hour, we can compute the unit rate of liters of water lost per hour. We do this by dividing the number of liters, $6,$ by the number of hours, $\dfrac 23$, as follows:

\[ 6 \div \dfrac 23 \]

To divide by a fraction, we multiply by the fraction's reciprocal:

\begin{align} 6\div \dfrac 23&= 6\times \dfrac{3}{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{6}{1} \times \dfrac{3}{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{6 \times 3}{1 \times 2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{18}{2} \\[5pt] &= 9 \end{align}

Therefore, the pool will lose $9$ liters of water in $1$ hour.

question.text: At a fair, a carousel makes $3$ revolutions in $\dfrac35$ minutes. How many revolutions does it make in $1$ minute?
question.explanation:
To find out the number of revolutions the carousel makes in $1$ minute, we can compute the unit rate of revolutions per minute. We do this by dividing the number of revolutions, $3,$ by the number of minutes, $\dfrac 35$, as follows:

\[ 3 \div \dfrac 35 \]

To divide by a fraction, we multiply by the fraction's reciprocal:

\begin{align} 3\div \dfrac 35&= 3\times \dfrac{5}{3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{1} \times \dfrac{5}{3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3 \times 5}{1 \times 3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{15}{3} \\[5pt] &= 5 \end{align}

Therefore, the carousel makes $5$ revolutions in $1$ minute.

question.text: Owen takes $\dfrac{4}{5}$ hours to do $24$ math exercises. How many exercises can he do in $1$ hour?
question.explanation:
To find the number of exercises Owen can do in $1$ hour, we compute the unit rate of exercises per hour. We do this by dividing the number of exercises Owen does, $24,$ by the number of hours, $\dfrac{4}{5},$ as follows:

\[ 24\div \dfrac{4}{5} \]

Dividing a fraction by a whole number is equivalent to multiplying the fraction by the reciprocal of that whole number:

\begin{align} 24\div \dfrac{4}{5}&= 24 \times \dfrac{5}{4} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{24}{1} \times \dfrac{5}{4} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{24 \times 5}{1 \times 4} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{120}{4}\\[5pt] &=30 \end{align}

Therefore, Owen can do $30$ exercises in $1$ hour.

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating a Unit Rate as the Quotient of a Fraction and an Integer

question.text: A plane can travel $\dfrac35$ of a mile in $6$ seconds. What is the unit rate of miles traveled per second?
question.explanation:
To compute the unit rate of miles per second, we divide the number of miles, $\dfrac{3}{5},$ by the number of seconds, $6$, as follows:

\[ \dfrac{3}{5} \div 6 \]

Dividing a fraction by a whole number is equivalent to multiplying the fraction by the reciprocal of that whole number:

\begin{align} \require{cancel} \dfrac{3}{5} \div 6&= \dfrac{3}{5} \div \dfrac {6}{1}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{5} \times \dfrac{1}{6} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3 \times 1}{5 \times 6} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{{3} \times 1}{5 \times 2\times {3}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\cancel{3} \times 1}{5 \times 2\times \cancel{3}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{10} \end{align}

Therefore, the unit rate in this situation is $ \dfrac{1}{10} $ miles per second.

example.title: Calculating a Unit Rate as the Quotient of a Fraction and an Integer

question.text: Johnny walked $\dfrac 38$ of a mile in $ 7$ minutes, keeping an even pace. How many miles did he walk in $1$ minute?
question.explanation:
To compute the number of miles Johnny walked in $1$ minute, we can compute the unit rate of miles per minute. We do this by dividing the number of miles, $\dfrac{3}{8},$ by the number of minute, as follows:

\[ \dfrac{3}{8} \div 7 \]

Dividing a fraction by a whole number is equivalent to multiplying the fraction by the reciprocal of that whole number:

\begin{align} \require{cancel} \dfrac{3}{8} \div 7&= \dfrac{3}{8} \times \dfrac{1}{7} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3 \times 1}{8 \times 7} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{56} \end{align}

So, Johnny walked $ \dfrac{3}{56} $ miles in $1$ minute.

question.text: A race car covers $\dfrac45$ of a lap in $2$ minutes. What is the unit rate of laps covered per minute?
question.explanation:
To compute the unit rate of laps per minute, we divide the number of laps, $\dfrac{4}{5},$ by the number of seconds, $2$, as follows:

\[ \dfrac{4}{5} \div 2 \]

Dividing a fraction by a whole number is equivalent to multiplying the fraction by the reciprocal of that whole number:

\begin{align} \require{cancel} \dfrac{4}{5} \div 2&= \dfrac{4}{5} \div \dfrac {2}{1}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4}{5} \times \dfrac{1}{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4 \times 1}{5 \times 2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{{2} \times 2}{2 \times 5 } \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\cancel{2} \times 2}{\cancel{2} \times 5 } \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{5} \end{align}

Therefore, the unit rate in this situation is $ \dfrac{2}{5} $ laps per minute.

question.text: An air compressor moves $\dfrac{8}{15}$ gallons of air in four seconds. Find the unit rate of gallons per second.
question.explanation:
To compute the unit rate of gallons per second, we divide the number of gallons, $\dfrac{8}{15},$ by the number of seconds, $4$, as follows:

\[ \dfrac{8}{15} \div 4 \]

Dividing a fraction by a whole number is equivalent to multiplying the fraction by the reciprocal of that whole number:

\begin{align} \require{cancel} \dfrac{8}{15} \div 4&= \dfrac{8}{15} \div \dfrac 41\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{8}{15} \times \dfrac{1}{4} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{8 \times 1}{15 \times 4} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2 \times 4}{15 \times 4} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2 \times \cancel{4}}{15 \times \cancel{4}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{15} \end{align}

Therefore, the unit rate in this situation is $\dfrac{2}{15} $ gallons per second.

question.text: A pump moves $\dfrac{9}{10}$ gallons of water in three minutes. Find the unit rate of gallons per minute.
question.explanation:
To compute the unit rate of gallons per minute, we divide the number of gallons, $\dfrac{9}{10},$ by the number of minutes, $3$, as follows:

\[ \dfrac{9}{10} \div 3 \]

Dividing a fraction by a whole number is equivalent to multiplying the fraction by the reciprocal of that whole number:

\begin{align} \require{cancel} \dfrac{9}{10} \div 3&= \dfrac{9}{10} \div \dfrac 31\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{9}{10} \times \dfrac{1}{3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{9 \times 1}{10 \times 3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3\times 3}{10\times 3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3\times \cancel{3} }{10 \times\cancel{3}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{10} \end{align}

Therefore, the unit rate in this situation is $ \dfrac{3}{10} $ gallons per minute.

question.text: A container with $\dfrac{3}{4}$ gallons of weed killer can spray $\dfrac{7}{4}$ lawns. What is the unit rate of gallons per lawn?
question.explanation:
To compute the unit rate of gallons per lawn, we divide the number of gallons, $\dfrac 34,$ by the number of lawns, $\dfrac 74$, as follows: \[ \dfrac{3}{4} \div \dfrac74 \]

Dividing a fraction by another fraction is equivalent to multiplying the first fraction by the reciprocal of the second fraction:

\begin{align} \require{cancel} \dfrac{3}{4} \div \dfrac74 &= \dfrac{3}{4} \times \dfrac{4}{7} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3 \times 4}{4 \times 7} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3\times\cancel{4}}{\cancel{4} \times 7} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{7} \end{align}

Therefore, the unit rate is $\dfrac{3}{7}$ gallons per lawn.

example.title: Calculating a Unit Rate as the Quotient of a Fraction and a Fraction

question.text: Riding his electric bike, Matt can go $\dfrac 12$ of a mile in $\dfrac 34$ minutes. What is the unit rate of miles covered per minute?
question.explanation:
To compute the unit rate of miles per minute, we divide the number of miles, $\dfrac 12,$ by the number of minutes, $\dfrac 34$, as follows: \[ \dfrac{1}{2} \div \dfrac34 \]

Dividing a fraction by another fraction is equivalent to multiplying the first fraction by the reciprocal of the second fraction:

\begin{align} \require{cancel} \dfrac{1}{2} \div \dfrac34 &= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{4}{3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1 \times 4}{2 \times 3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2 \times 2}{2 \times 3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\cancel{2 } \times 2}{\cancel{2} \times 3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{align}

Therefore, the unit rate is $\dfrac 23$ miles per minute.

example.title: Calculating a Unit Rate as the Quotient of a Fraction and a Fraction

question.text: A skydiver falls $\dfrac 45$ of a mile in $\dfrac 25$ minutes. What is the unit rate of miles fallen per minute?
question.explanation:
To compute the unit rate of miles per minute, we divide the number of miles, $\dfrac 45,$ by the number of minutes, $\dfrac 25$, as follows: \[ \dfrac{4}{5} \div \dfrac25 \]

Dividing a fraction by another fraction is equivalent to multiplying the first fraction by the reciprocal of the second fraction:

\begin{align} \require{cancel} \dfrac{4}{5} \div \dfrac25 &= \dfrac{4}{5} \times \dfrac{5}{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4 \times 5}{5 \times 2} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2 \times 2\times 5}{5\times 2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\cancel{2}\times\cancel{5} \times 2}{\cancel{2} \times \cancel{5}} \\[5pt] &= 2 \end{align}

Therefore, the unit rate is $2$ miles per minute.

example.title: Calculating a Unit Rate as the Quotient of a Fraction and a Fraction

question.text: A certain satellite makes $\dfrac 13$ of its orbit around the Earth in $\dfrac 16$ of a day. How many times can it orbit Earth in $1$ day?
question.explanation:
To find how many times the satellite can go around the Earth in $1$ day, we can compute the orbital unit rate per day. We do this by dividing the amount of the orbit the satellite travels, $\dfrac{1}{3},$ by the corresponding fraction of a day, $\dfrac{1}{6},$ as follows:

\[ \dfrac{1}{3} \div \dfrac{1}{6} \]

Dividing a fraction by another fraction is equivalent to multiplying the first fraction by the reciprocal of the second fraction:

\begin{align} \dfrac{1}{3} \div \dfrac{1}{6} &= \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{6}{1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1 \times 6}{3 \times 1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{6}{3}\\[5pt] &=2 \end{align}

Therefore, the satellite can orbit Earth $2 $ times in $1$ day.

example.title: Calculating a Unit Rate as the Quotient of a Fraction and a Fraction

question.text: Jim ran $\dfrac{5}{6}$ of a mile in $\dfrac{1}{5}$ of an hour. How many miles can Jim run in $1$ hour?
question.explanation:
To find the number of miles Jim can run in $1$ hour, we can compute the unit rate of miles per hour. We do this by dividing the number of miles, $\dfrac{5}{6},$ by the number of hours, $\dfrac{1}{5},$ as follows:

\[ \dfrac{5}{6} \div \dfrac{1}{5} \]

Dividing a fraction by another fraction is equivalent to multiplying the first fraction by the reciprocal of the second fraction:

\begin{align} \dfrac{5}{6} \div \dfrac{1}{5} &= \dfrac{5}{6} \times \dfrac{5}{1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5 \times 5}{6 \times 1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{25}{6} \end{align}

Finally, we write the resulting improper fraction as a mixed number:

\[ \dfrac{25}{6} = 4 \, \textrm{R} 1 = 4 \, \dfrac{1}{6} \]

Therefore, Jim can run $4 \, \dfrac{1}{6}$ miles in $1$ hour.
